context: Dante stands in its golden center, looking up and around at the tiers of the blessed.

note: The Church, meaning all the saved. The Bible calls it the bride of Christ, and says he won it with his own blood on the cross.

context: They fly without rest between God above and the souls seated in the Rose.

note: The angels go down into the Rose like bees into a flower and return to God as to the hive. Unlike bees they do not take anything from the flower: they bring peace and love down to it.
The three colors are usually read as signs: the flame-red faces for burning love, the gold wings for wisdom, the white for purity.
The peace and burning love that the angels draw from God as they fly up to him, and then share with the souls.

The poem's opening idea, stated again near its end: God's light shines through everything, more in one thing and less in another, as each is fit to receive it (Paradiso 1). A crowd of angels casts no shadow in it.
The saved from before Christ, the people of the Old Testament, and those from after. Canto 32 shows how the two groups are seated.

context: The blessed see the three persons as one single star. Dante breaks off his description to pray for the troubled world he has left.

note: Life on earth, and the wars and corruption of Dante's Italy in particular.

The far north. Helice, also called Callisto, was a nymph loved by Jupiter and changed into a bear, then set in the sky as the Great Bear. Her son Arcas became a constellation beside her. In northern lands the Bear circles overhead and never sets.
A palace in Rome, later the home of the popes. It stands here for the city at the height of its splendor, when northern tribesmen first saw it and stood amazed.

context: The third contrast lands as a blow: Heaven is to Florence as the divine is to the human and eternity is to time. This is the last time the poem names Dante's city.

note: A pilgrim who has reached the shrine he swore to visit, and looks around so as to describe it at home. Dante has called himself a pilgrim throughout, and Heaven is the end of his road.
He has taken in the whole shape of the Rose. Its detailed plan, with who sits where, is given in Canto 32.
Saint Bernard, who gives his name at line 111. Beatrice has gone back to her seat without a word, much as Virgil slipped away when she arrived (Purgatorio 30). This time there is no grief.

context: Her work as guide is done. She has returned to her own place in the Rose and sent Bernard to lead Dante the last step.

note: The third row counting down from the top. Mary sits in the first, Eve in the second, and Beatrice in the third beside Rachel (Canto 32).
She is farther from him than the top of the sky is from the bottom of the sea. Yet he sees her perfectly, because in the Empyrean nothing lies between and distance does not dim.

Dante's farewell and thanks to Beatrice, the last words he speaks to her. In the Italian he calls her "tu", the familiar form of "you", for the first time. Until now he has always used the respectful "voi".
She went down to Limbo to ask Virgil to rescue Dante from the dark wood (Inferno 2).
From the slavery of sin to a free and upright will. Virgil told Cato at the foot of Purgatory that Dante was seeking freedom (Purgatorio 1).
He asks that he may keep the health she has given him until he dies, so that his soul may come back here.
Her last look at him. She then turns back to God, and Dante does not speak to her again.
God, the source from which all light and joy flow.
Beatrice's request and her love for Dante brought Bernard down from his seat.

context: Bernard was famous for his devotion to her. It is through her that Dante will be given the sight of God.
Virgil stood for what reason can reach and Beatrice for what faith teaches. The last step is to see God directly, and for that Dante is given a man known for contemplation and for love of Mary.

note: For an Italian, a distant land: any pilgrim who has come a very long way.

A cloth kept at Saint Peter's in Rome and believed to show the true face of Christ, printed on it when a woman wiped his face on the way to the cross. It was shown to crowds of pilgrims. Dante looks at Bernard as such a pilgrim looks at the face he has heard of all his life.
Bernard was believed to have had, in prayer, a foretaste on earth of the peace of Heaven.
Mary sits at the highest point of the Rose's rim. Dante has to raise his eyes from the bottom of the flower to its farthest edge.

context: The place meant is the point on the eastern horizon where the sun's chariot is about to rise, the brightest part of the sky at dawn.

note: Dante's word is oriafiamma, the oriflamme: the red and gold battle standard of the kings of France. Mary's part of the Rose is a golden flame too, but a banner of peace, not of war.

quote: each different in radiance and nature
note: Thomas Aquinas taught that no two angels are of the same kind: each one is a species to itself.
Mary. Dante does not describe her, and says only that her smile was the joy in all the other faces.
Throughout Paradise Dante has learned by watching the one he loves look at something higher. Bernard's gaze at Mary now does for him what Beatrice's gaze did before.
